title: Deciding first-order definability of orbit-finite automata
formal: Is it decidable, given a finitely presented deterministic orbit-finite automaton over an infinite equality-only data alphabet \(D\), whether its language \(L\subseteq D^*\) is definable by a first-order sentence using the order of word positions and equality of their data values?
why: Over finite alphabets, first-order definability has a classical effective algebraic characterization. This problem asks whether that connection remains decidable when finite memory stores data from an infinite set, beyond the narrower orbit-finite-monoid setting.
status_note: The 2011 paper and its 2013 journal version explicitly leave the deterministic orbit-finite-automaton problem open. A bounded later-work check on 13 September 2026 did not locate a resolution. The finite presentation makes the input model explicit; newer decidability results for first-order properties of orbit-finite structures are not treated as answers to this language-definability question.

progress.text: Bojańczyk proves the first-order/aperiodicity characterization for orbit-finite syntactic data monoids and poses decidability for the larger deterministic orbit-finite-automaton class.
The journal version, Nominal Monoids, retains the deterministic-automaton definability question and the proposed aperiodicity criterion.

importance.reason: A foundational definability boundary for nominal automata, connecting effective algebra and infinite-alphabet language theory while isolating the deterministic finite-orbit restriction.

sentences: The alphabet consists of infinitely many data values that can only be compared for equality.
The deterministic automaton has finitely many kinds of state up to renaming stored data.
The target is an algorithm deciding whether a sentence about position order and data equality defines its entire language.
The known orbit-finite-monoid characterization applies to a smaller class than the automata in this question.
A proposed aperiodicity characterization would need an effective test before it could establish decidability.

definitions: Fix a countably infinite set \(D\), whose elements have no structure except equality. A data word is a finite sequence \(w=d_1\cdots d_n\), including the empty word. A data permutation is a bijection \(D\to D\). The automaton consists of a state set \(Q\) acted on by all data permutations, an initial state \(q_0\) fixed by every permutation, a set of final states \(F\), and a total deterministic transition function \(\delta:Q\times D\to Q\). Both \(F\) and \(\delta\) are equivariant: renaming all data values preserves finality and commutes with transitions. Every state has finite support, meaning a finite set of data values whose pointwise fixation fixes the state. Orbit-finite means that renaming data partitions \(Q\) into finitely many equivalence classes. Acceptance starts at \(q_0\), follows the unique transition sequence and tests finality after the last letter. The finite input presentation is as follows. Each state orbit has an integer arity \(r\geq0\) and a finite subgroup \(H\) of the permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\). Its states are injective \(r\)-tuples of data, identified under coordinate permutations from \(H\). The presentation lists the orbit tags, arities, groups, final tags and a zero-arity initial tag. A finite transition table gives a target tag and a tuple of selectors from the old coordinates and current input datum for each possible equality case between that datum and the coordinates. Selected output coordinates must be distinct, and the rules must be compatible with the stated coordinate identifications. These finite consistency conditions ensure a well-defined equivariant function; no unseen data value may be generated. Thus unordered stored data sets as well as ordered registers are represented, without an infinite transition table. A first-order formula quantifies only over the positions \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), has the usual Boolean operations and quantifiers, position equality and order \(<\), and the relation \(i\sim j\) interpreted as \(d_i=d_j\). There are no named data constants, data-order tests, predicates for arithmetic on positions or quantifiers over sets. Definability means that one finite sentence accepts exactly the language for all word lengths and all data values. Decidability asks for one deterministic Turing machine halting on every valid finite automaton presentation; no complexity bound is specified.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating algorithm deciding this first-order definability question for every valid presented automaton. Alternatively prove in Lean that the decision problem is undecidable. An algebraic characterization counts as a decision procedure only with an effective test for its condition on these inputs. A theorem assuming that the syntactic monoid itself is orbit-finite covers only a restricted class.

context_blocks.text: An orbit represents all states that differ only in the actual names of stored data. Remembering one datum requires infinitely many concrete states but only one such state orbit. Finite orbit count bounds the shape of memory without bounding the number of possible input data values.

The source’s example “the first datum appears again later” is recognized by a deterministic orbit-finite automaton: it can retain the first datum and remember whether another occurrence has appeared. The same property is first-order definable by selecting the first position and a later position carrying equal data.

The 2011 theorem characterizes first-order definability when the syntactic data monoid is orbit-finite. The source explicitly asks to extend decidability to orbit-finite deterministic automata, whose syntactic monoids need not have finitely many orbits. The first-datum example already demonstrates the difference between these hypotheses.

The syntactic monoid identifies words \(u,v\) when \(xuy\in L\) iff \(xvy\in L\) for every pair of context words \(x,y\); multiplication is concatenation of equivalence classes. A monoid is aperiodic when each element \(m\) satisfies \(m^k=m^{k+1}\) for some integer \(k\geq1\). In an infinite monoid this definition does not silently impose one common exponent for all elements.

The author conjectures aperiodicity as the appropriate condition in the larger deterministic-automaton class. It is a candidate characterization, not an established algorithm in the source. The paper also gives a language outside the relevant restricted setting for which aperiodicity does not imply first-order definability.

Undecidability for first-order definability from nondeterministic register automata is a different input problem. The present automata have one unique run. Likewise, deciding a first-order property of the automaton’s state structure is different from deciding whether some first-order sentence defines its entire word language.
